Ringside Gel Boxing MMA Hand Wraps Just like the larger set I was looking forward to getting these gel boxing wraps to review, the small was one I originally thought might fit me, but it turns out the large was fine. The small is very small. I tried them on, but could not fasten the Velcro around my wrist properly and it was tight around my hand. So definitely pay attention to the sizing chart. Measure Around your palm. That is the most important part of the size. I’m not a fan of pink, but my daughter does. I handed them over to her to try out.
So this is what my daughter said about the wraps. “these are super comfortable Mom”.
She liked them so much she wore them all evening, even after hitting the bag a few times.
The gel is very comfortable. And I like that she can hit the heavy bag easily with no damage to her small hands. I like boxing drills with the heavy bag for endurance and traditional wraps are too big for my daughter. I know from experience that while you can toss these in the wash, sometimes the gel doesn’t allow it to get super clean that way. Sometimes soap gets trapped behind the gel, or it just never stops smelling faintly of mold or the gym. So I usually hand wash my gel wraps, gloves, and accessories and hang to dry. It’s not a deal breaker. And it’s not that hard. But cold wash for sure.
text_fidelity_b: Ringside Gel Boxing MMA Hand Wraps

Part of the reason for that is that I did purchase one of their "Zombie Killer" knives and was sorely disappointed in the design, balance and durability. But it was obvious that the review I wrote ruffled the feathers of some die-hard Ka-Bar fans who evidently didn't understand what attributes a dependable knife should have.

This knife is a way different animal than the "Zombie Killer" and is an example of a great knife. The design, balance, and mostly durable construction make for a good tool to carry whatever the need. It is comfortable to hold, has a razor sharp blade, and just feels right in the hand. Anyone facing this knife knows that the threat is not to be taken lightly--especially in the hands of an expert.

The one concern I have is where the full tang of the blade becomes thinner where it enters the handle. I tend to be rough on my tools and depend on them to perform as needed. This particular construction creates a weak area if the knife is used for leverage. I don't want to be let down by a broken knife, but most owners will not put it through the paces that I would. My fishing partner's Simms have sprung a leak that was not fixed after repair. The bottom line is that if you get a good pair of these waders, they are as good as ones costing twice as much.

text_fidelity_a:
Cold Steel Pocket Bushman Just received this knife as a gift from Cold Steel Special Projects. I had ordered a discontinued Spectre ($400 knife for $100)directly from them but the final shipment didn't meet their standards. As an apology, they shipped me a Pocket Bushman. By the way, the Special Projects web site offers great deals on discontinued models (like the Rajah) for significant savings.
My first thought was "what's a Pocket Bushman?". That was quickly answered when I slid it out of the box. Very strong and utilitarian looking tool. But I still didn't really get it until it opened with a bang and locked up fast and tight. It's just over 10 inches long when opened with a 4 inch razor sharp (and I mean RAZOR SHARP)blade. I told my wife that it was sharp enough to shave with and then immediately cut myself by trying to close it without looking at the instructions. You'd think that I would be smarter than that at my age. One quick swipe and the tip of my index finger started leaking blood through a cut that you could barely see. Blood everywhere.

This is a big cumbersome tool that will handle any task you set it to. Cold Steel's motto seems to be "If it's worth doing, it's worth overdoing". If you have to pull it out in a defensive situation, your opponent is going to think twice about engaging you. The intimidation factor is impressive--and it inspires confidence in your hand. Take my word for it. It's not for amateurs and will do accidental damage quickly.
"If you find yourself in a fair fight, your tactics suck!"
text_fidelity_b: Cold Steel Pocket Bushman

text_fidelity_a:
Omron HJ-203 Pedometer with Activity Tracker The Omron is quiet small and light. I can have it in a pocket along with my wallet or iPhone and I don't notice it's there. But I'm skeptical about its accuracy.

I took a few walks and compared the distance it recorded with the route mapped out as a walk in Google Maps. The Omron would typically under measure my distance anywhere from 30 to 60 percent. I re-checked the height, weight and stride settings but that had no effect. I guess it's unrealistic that a pedometer can accurately measure distance.

A more serious flaw is that the unit does not keep lifetime stats -- it's memory is only 7 days. If you have a workout schedule where you need to keep a log of your daily steps, the 7 day memory feature is quite nice for when you forget to write down a day's results, but I would think most people would like to know how many steps they've taken after a year.

While I suppose the distance issue is forgivable -- most people buy a pedometer to keep track of steps, not miles traveled -- the lack of lifetime memory makes it hard to recommend this unit.
text_fidelity_b: Omron HJ-203 Pedometer with Activity Tracker

text_fidelity_a:
Snowshoes for Adult Unisex,Fully Adjustable Bindings, Lightweight Material, Hard Pack Grip Teeth,Outdoor Aluminum Alloy Material Really like these snowshoes. They are easy to adjust and stay on very well. The bag the shoes came in is first rate as are the poles. My only complaint is that the front binding only ratchets to a point then seem to hang up (it could be the strap end catching on the decking, or perhaps the hard boot material failing to flex)not a huge deal because it is snug enough. Also the pole carrying bag is separate from the shoe bag which means I got to remember to grab both. All in all a nice inexpensive snowshoe. Great for beginners or someone just needing a cheaper option.
12/29/11 UPDATE_ Got to try these out for the first time (not real deep snow- but enough to give them a trial run) These shoes are really nice. I tromped around for about 30 mins and had very few problems (main problem was some ice build up on my heel as I crossed a wet area and the water froze on my boot heel- not a big deal as it can happen with any snowshoe). The bindings did hold well and did not loosen at all. One shoe did seem to be toeing in a bit but that was probably an adjustment issue (it was also a new pair of boots I was trying out.) I'm gonna hopefully get out in some deeper snow next week (yea Lake Effect!)
1/15/12 UPDATE2- Finally got some REAL snow (18+ inches!) and tried these out at my hilly property in the deep woods. AMAZING how well they worked. It was pretty cold (hovering around 16° F in the sun) and the woods were untouched by anything but a few deer and turkeys. These shoes performed great. They never slipped and I did not have to adjust the bindings at all. They do seem to make a bit of noise as far as the bindings creaking (at these temps not to surprising), but nothing broke or loosened. Walked for a little over an hour; over logs, thru brush, uphill, downhill, level, tight twisty area, open fields, deep drifts, and even a snowmobile trail (that crosses the front of our property). These preformed as good as any other shoe. A bonus is I found I really liked the poles- so much so that I gave one to my wife and she really liked using it too. All in all a great purchase- These honestly hover on a 5 star rating- I did have to take away for the pole bag not being attached some way- also the poles are nearly impossible to closeup once they get cold (I think a bit of frost gets into the loosening cam and freezes the pole in place as once they warmed up there were no problems) also there is no place to store the rubber protection cap from the pole. The one show still seemed to toe in a bit- but I only notice it in very shallow snow (less than 6 inches) and the toe binding still only rachets to a certain point and then slips (still not an issue as it is snug enough). Oh and of course the noise factor (not real bad but your not gonna sneak up on anything with these on)
text_fidelity_b: Snowshoes for Adult Unisex,Fully Adjustable Bindings, Lightweight Material, Hard Pack Grip Teeth,Outdoor Aluminum Alloy Material

Foxelli Trekking Poles – 2-pc Pack Collapsible Lightweight Hiking Poles, Strong Aircraft Aluminum Adjustable Walking Sticks with Natural Cork Grips and 4 Season All Terrain Accessories The hiking poles are so cool! I have had MS for a bit over 30 years and have been using a cane to help with balance but it is unwieldy and has me listing to one side. I believe that using these two hiking poles will improve my posture, give me more sensory input to help me maintain my balance and thus, making it easier to walk further, especially on uneven ground.

The hiking poles come with directions to adjust the poles to the correct length and how to check for stability. There is a chart to give the length of the poles and the poles have the the corresponding numbers printed on them to facilitate adjustment. The grips fit my hands nicely. The poles are light weight and remarkably sturdy.

I am looking forward to trying them out at the beach using the snow tips. My cane and walker are both useless in soft sand. I like that I can get replacement tips if necessary.

I’m attending a wedding out of state next month at a farm/barn type wedding venue. I’m sure these poles will help me maintain my balance on uneven ground better and reduce my fear of falling. I’m probably not ever going to hike the Appalachian trail but these poles will help me to be less fearful of walking on uneven ground.

The shape is a bit asymmetric and fits well within my hand. Good capacity (about 18 fluid ounces). I also like that you can use the dishwasher to clean the bottle--many other bottles advise to handwash them.

This is an expensive water bottle. The bottle by itself is worth only a fraction of the price. The one feature that makes it worth buying the Water-to-Go bottle is its filter that is advertised as removing not just superficial dirt, but microscopic viruses, bacteria, parasites, pesticides, etc. Unfortunately I don't have the skillset to personally test whether "99.9999% of water-borne contaminants" are actually removed by the filter. I've read several external reviews, but I haven't seen an independent scientific, technical test of the filtering system. If the filtering system is as good as advertised, then I am OK with paying the high price of the bottle + filter. In long hikes, it is highly valuable to carry less weight because most of your water needs can be met by refilling this bottle.

text_fidelity_a:
Suunto 3 Fitness Tracker Sports Watch This is a great fitness watch, but it's not that good of a smart watch. I wouldn't suggest cross shopping this with a Samsung Gear or Apple Watch, as they can do quite a bit more than this. Likewise some of the newer Garmin watches are a bit more capable, but if you're looking for a fitness watch (with some smart watch features), this is a very good option.

It sets up quickly, although the charger is more akin to what I expected from 2015 than 2018. It clips on, and it charges reasonably quickly. It has a guided setup and decent instructions that will help walk you through using the watch. I'd rely on those, as it's not the most intuitive watch. Apple and Samsung have them beat there (I haven't used a Garmin). In regards to use, I find the GPS to be quite accurate (compared to phone) and the heart rate and steps to be accurate (compared to a Fitbit). Both do well compared to my own non-scientific tests (ie the heart rate looked right and the recorded journey matched my recollection).

I would say that a Samsung, Apple (if you use iPhones), and Garmin would be more broadly recommended. This is a bit of a fitness watch for fit people (the Garmin fits the bill there), and it's not a "lifestyle accessory" or gizmo. I found the focus on fitness to be refreshing and a bit of a reminder of what I'm trying to do, but I couldn't send tunes to my earbuds or other stuff I can do with some of my other watches. I find it to be a solid tradeoff, but it may not be for you.

4 stars for being a bit niche but not being absolutely amazing at that niche.
text_fidelity_b: Suunto 3 Fitness Tracker Sports Watch

text_fidelity_a:
WATERFLY Lightweight Packable Hiking Backpack： Foldable Travel Daypack Ultralight Camping Day Pack for Woman Man Out of the starting gate, I will say, I did consider giving this backpack a 4 star rather than 5 based on the shoulder straps. They are not that thickly padded, so that is something to seriously consider, but that said, my wife and I do like this bag and so far feel like we’ll get great use out of it. But because the straps are not that padded we would use this as our backup pack on longer days and trips - rather than the main one. The bag itself does give us the space we want and need, but the straps really should be thicker for more comfort.

So...
1. We like the color - it’s a nice blue and works with our gear.
2. We like that it can fold down literally into itself - it is a bag that opens and has the backpack attached then folds back down into itself. It’s great and easy to store or take inside another bag.
3. It opens and closes down easily and quickly - well, it takes a couple times to figure out how best to close down into itself - but once you do it, you’ve got it.
4. It holds a decent amount of stuff. If you’re doing a day hike, like to just get out from time to time, even for those days with the family (theme parks, parks, beach, etc) you can find this as a very nice bag to carry that extra stuff you want and need.
5. It has some nice smaller sections to put those little things you don’t want to loose.
6. There is one of those headphone holes. I seriously have no clue what people do with those. We use wireless headgear, so we don’t have the cords to attach - I think I’d forget I’m connected THROUGH that hole and rip the thing off my head if I took that pack off and it was attached. So for me - I have no need. But it is there if you want it and we think we figured out the little pouch you’d put your phone into. But even there - I wouldn’t want my phone inside the bag - I’d want it on the outside, easier to get to. But that’s me.

Overall this is a nice, lite easy to pack backpack. No, it’s likely not one you’re going to use if you’re into major hiking or camping. But it’s one you’d take with for once you’re out there, you can pull this out and take your day hikes with it. There is no frame - we are not campers or major hikers, but I understand frames are often wanted/preferred. We do like this and will get use out of it. Happy to have found.
text_fidelity_b: WATERFLY Lightweight Packable Hiking Backpack： Foldable Travel Daypack Ultralight Camping Day Pack for Woman Man

text_fidelity_a:
Coast DX355 Double Lock Folding Knife I've been looking for a folding knife that I could use around the farm. This knife is 4.5 inches long and 1.5 inches wide when folded, so it has a nice sized blade while still being small enough not to get in my way when clipped onto my pocket. (There is a strong, nearly 3-inch-long metal clip securely screwed into the knife handle.) The entire knife appears to be made out of a sturdy, stainless steel. The handle has a texture and finger indentations to assure a secure grip when used.

I've never used a folding knife with a locking mechanism, but I expected at least some advertising pointing out how the special double-locking mechanism works. There wasn't any information included with the knife, but it was fairly easy to figure out. The linear lock is beneath the blade and automatically locks when the blade is fully extended. The safety switch is a toggle on the handle behind the blade. You can push it up when the blade is open to prevent the linear lock from being depressed (which would allow the blade to close). To close the blade, push the toggle back to the original position and depress the linear lock while folding the blade. Once I figured it out, it was easy to do.

Since it's winter, I haven't had much time to test the blade out for how well it keeps it edge or other wear issues. I'll post an update is anything significant comes up.
text_fidelity_b: Coast DX355 Double Lock Folding Knife

CyclingDeal Bike Bicycle Cargo Rack - Great for 26" 27.5, 700c & 29" Adjustable Touring Rear Back of Bike Carrier - Pannier Luggage Rack with Extended Wings - Light Aluminum - Load Limit 55 lbs/25kg I don't know why this style of rack isn't everywhere, I've never found another one like it. The sides swing out and lock very, very securely, it was easy to fit to my belt-drive Ebike (ride1up V2 roadster) I only had to mount it inside the frame posts instead of outside. Other than that, some gentle bending of the seat post rods to maneuver around the rim brake caliper (they're good quality aluminum so bend them gently and slowly) and the rack fit right on the bike. It can hold a ton of weight, I've put enough groceries on the thing to make the bike quite literally not sit with the front wheel on the ground.

It's also plenty sturdy enough to pick the bike up by, I've been using the front of the rack as a hand hold for over a year now, climbing/descending multiple flights of stairs a day and the wings are still smooth and the finish pristine, despite 5 days a week hanging off the back end of a Fast Ferry, getting soaked in saltwater.

The post spacing and overall shape are perfect for a variety of panniers. I have a few different kinds with hooks and straps, and it's accepted them all. The only thing I might want different is it'd be nice if the wings locked in the down position - as it is, they just stay down with friction, which is fine unless you want to use the wing as a hook point for a bungee strap, in which case it will open up, so you have to go lower for a hook point. text_fidelity_a:
Kuat Dirtbag This mount was exactly what I needed. I had built a fork mount roof rack for my fatbike out of an old Thule rack. I originally used a sunlite fatbike fork mount, but after the nut fell off that mount and not being able to buy a new one, I had to replace the whole unit.
I bought the 135mm X 9mm fork mount. This fits fatbike forks with 135mm spacing with quick release. I have. 2014 Specialized fatboy and it fits perfect. It won't fit through axle forks like the Bluto which are 150mm X 15mm. This mount does not come with a 135mm skewer, so you can either buy an extra, or use the one from your wheel. The rear wheels of most mountain bikes is 135mm so they are pretty common and affordable. The fork rests on two short metal tubes the same size as your axle, and just like your axle the skewer goes through the metal tubes to anchor your fork to the mount. This design is ingenious. There has been mention of misalignment in other reviews, mine did not have that problem. If the skewer falls off or someone steals it, you only have to replace the skewer and not the whole unit. This mount is good quality and should last awhile.
text_fidelity_b: Kuat Dirtbag

Sportline Lightweight Walking Advantage 385 Tally Counter With Easy To Read Number Display That Counts Up To 9999 Anyone working out on an indoor track will find a counter helpful. At 12 laps a mile, counting laps is difficult. Counting is easy; remembering how many laps I've done is hard.

The Sportline counter fixes what my math teacher could not, allowing me to turn my mental energies toward my workout, or toward a conversation with my running partner.

---Necessary on a Practical Level---
I tried a system of using my fingers on my right hand to measure laps 1-5, then using my left hand to measure how many laps in groups of five. That is, two fingers on my left and three fingers on my right would equal 13 laps. It sounds easier to employ than it actually is.

The Sportline counter has five worthwhile features:
* It counts one per click, up to 9,999. I won't run more than that, so, for me, it is plenty.
* The display is legible while running. The white digits are large, on a black background.
* The size of the device is small enough to carry.
* The finger loop fits nicely in my middle finger.
* The reset dial quickly zeroes out the counter.

The only two drawbacks are
* The reset dial would be more comfortably located on the left, not the right side of the counter, or otherwise better engineered for right-handed users.
* The weight is heavy. It is small, but can feel like baggage during a longer workout.

The Sportline counter is sturdy, does as advertised, and serves well as a tool for anyone walking or running a lot of laps.

Anthony Trendl
[...]
text_fidelity_b: Sportline Lightweight Walking Advantage 385 Tally Counter With Easy To Read Number Display That Counts Up To 9999

text_fidelity_a:
RAD Sportz Kayak Hoist 2-Pack Quality Garage Storage Canoe Lift with 125 lb Capacity Even Works as Ladder Lift Premium Quality Pulley System 1. - determine which way your joists run if you have a finished garage. More than likely, they will run parallel to the garage doors, but you still need to locate them with a stud finder.
2. - If you are hanging your kayaks perpendicular to the joists, you will more than likely need to get a couple of 2X4s long enough to span the required length, and bolt them to the joists as there will not be enough surface area to attached the mounting brackets.
3. - Go to the home improvement store and buy (5) 3 1/2" X 5/16 lag bolts and washers to bolt the 2x4 to the ceiling. You need 3 1/2 inches to make sure you have enough to go thought the thickness of the 2x4 and the sheet rock. Buy replacement 2" x 1/4" lag bolts supplied with kit for the mounting bracket (four needed per kayak).
4. Attach 2x4s to ceiling making sure you hit the joists. Pre-drill with a bit one size smaller than the 5/16" lag bolt.
5. Follow the bracket placement directions provided in the instructions and attach brackets to ceiling.
6. The rest is as straight forward as you can get. The pulley system is self explanatory.
7. Attach the wall anchor using two of the supplied 1/4" lag bolts intended for the brackets in the kit. You should have these left over if you bought the replacements mentioned above. DO NOT use the screws provided. They sheared off while I was installing them.

Bolts are super cheap. I think they were 25 cents a piece and well worth the peace of mind. It's still a cheaper solution than trying to make it yourself.

Note #1: The weak point of the entire system is the little pins that attach the hooks to the pulley. If any one of these fail the entire yak will fall to the floor. I suggest a static safety strap or cable to run under the yaks when stored at each attachment point.
Note #2: This system will not lift the yak flush with the ceiling. It will be suspended a little low -16 to 18".
Note #3: Under no circumstance attempt to lift the kayak without first tying a taunt cord between the pulley brackes at either end. Otherwise, if you lift unevenly the straps will spread apart and the yak will fall (I learned this the hard way because I was impatient). See picture of yellow kayak. (I used reflective para cord for this instead of cutting the supplied black cord).
Tip - don't cut the black cord provided. leaving it connected prevents the cord from slipping through the pulley; especially on high ceilings. Basically, you will end up with a loop at the wall end if you didn't cut it and did it right.
text_fidelity_b: RAD Sportz Kayak Hoist 2-Pack Quality Garage Storage Canoe Lift with 125 lb Capacity Even Works as Ladder Lift Premium Quality Pulley System

TRIPLE TREE 30 OZ Vacuum Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle-Scratch Resistance & Eco-Friendly for Outdoor Sports, 850 ML Double Walled Construction Bottle (Black) [[VIDEOID:a948ab74a1bd5a1a9be7bc0535d12137]] This insulated stainless vacuum bottle does a good job keeping either hot or cold drinks at their desired temperature for several hours. The mouth is large enough to accept full-size ice cubes (see video), but also small enough to drink directly from it if you don't have a cup to pour your drink into. (You probably don't want to do that if you have really hot coffee in your bottle!)

I already own both Thermos and HydroFlask brand vacuum bottles, and the insulation ability of this Triple Tree version seems comparable (although I have not done a controlled test using identical temperature water in all three and monitoring temperatures over the course of a day or two). This is not a cheap imitation, though. I expect it would compare favorably in a real test. I can say that at the end of an 8-hour shift I still had a little bit of ice left in my water bottle, whenever I didn't drink all the water.

Part of what you pay for is packaging (see photo). Inside the Amazon shipping box was a corrugated cardboard box holding the bottle, which was in a foam sleeve to protect it from scratches. There was a little tag attached, and an advertising/instruction pamphlet. A fair (excessive?) amount of packaging. Maybe not a deal killer, but I put this in the minus column. There was also a spare silicone seal washer for the stopper top. That goes in the plus column, especially if I can find the washer when I need it in the (distant???) future.

The screw-top stopper has a small carabiner clipped onto the swiveling bail handle. The carabiner rattles against the metal bottle and makes some noise (maybe remove the carabiner for ninja work or bowhunting?). I think the carabiner may be useful for attaching the bottle to your pack, especially if you have one of those weak water bottle pockets on the side of your day pack. I find that water bottles don't stay in those pockets very well. This should help.

Overall, a decent insulated bottle that holds almost a quart. I'll keep using mine. Let me know if my review was helpful.
text_fidelity_b: TRIPLE TREE 30 OZ Vacuum Insulated Stainless Steel Water Bottle-Scratch Resistance & Eco-Friendly for Outdoor Sports, 850 ML Double Walled Construction Bottle (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Schwinn Fitness 140 Upright Exercise Bike (Discontinued) Like many others, I researched this bike for about 2 weeks before deciding to purchase it. I read everything I could find about Schwinn bikes period. The model before this (the 130) is what I was going to purchase at WalMart, it was cheaper but I would have to pay for tax & shipping (free shipping and no tax on Amazon.com) so it was only going to save me about $30 at WalMart (for the older model) so I am definitely glad I decided to buy the 140 at Amazon.com.
The previous model (130) was highly rated/recommended on the Consumer Report websites and that made me realize that a newer model would/should be even better. I live in a small apartment and although I wanted the recumbent one, I had to go with the upright. Not to mention, I figured I could work on my posture while riding upright. (ha ha) This bike is just what I need to get in shape. I have a leg injury and I am overweight and out of shape. I needed a piece of equipment that I could commit to and not feel like I was doing a dreaded chore. I can hop on this bike and watch tv, listen to music, talk with people around me, or just look out of my window.

At first I felt like the price was expensive compared to the other models, but it's true, you get what you pay for. As I mentioned, I am overweight and I needed something that would last while I pursued my fitness goals. The other brands are not built as well as the Schwinn models. Simply look at the frame work and tubing and you can tell.
After I put it together (without any problems whatsosever) I realized that it was of good quality and worth the money I spent. The setup was easy. I am a female with manicured nails and I didn't even chip my polish putting this bike together. I also didn't require any help. It was really easy. I had my laptop on my sofa with the manual enlarged (I went to the Schwinn website and downloaded it) so that I could see the images clearly, but I mainly used the paper manual that the bike came with.

I read the instructions for the setup of the user profile and everything went just fine.
~I read some reviews about little issues with customizing, but if you just take your time and read the manual, you will really see its not difficult. When you set up a custom workout, you have to realize that it goes through 30 levels so it appears as though nothing is happening, but be patient as you customize it and you will see that it is working right.~
~Also the Heart Rate monitor, if you simply plug it in on the side, it should work just fine. You just have to look for the spot to plug it in to.~
I have only used the bike 4 times so I can't give you any long term use information, other than the programs are nice, the resistance is great, and it has a lot of features on the console once you set up your user profile, but I can say that this is a very good investment for anyone considering purchasing a quality exercise bike. It is a good piece of equipment. If you have to save up a little to get the bike, start saving! If you are considering a different brand, forget about it! If you think that its hard to put together, get over the thought! If you are worried about it not being right for you, try it and you will like it!

I have a lot of weight to lose and I don't like going to the gym. I walk around my neighborhood which is ok, but now I can get a good little cardio workout. I am so glad that I got this bike. I am helping myself in the long run. This is the best way to spend over $300 and have something well worth it!

No missing/broken pieces, no damaged stabilizers, no damaged or flimsy box. I ordered and received in exactly 7 days. ***I'm NOT discrediting anyone's reviews about problems they had with their purchase, I am just stating that my purchase was problem free***

~I will add another review/or update in the future about how the bike is performing~ I hope this helps motivate someone!
text_fidelity_b: Schwinn Fitness 140 Upright Exercise Bike (Discontinued)

text_fidelity_a:
Condition 1 30” Case, Hard Lockable Storage Box, Water Resistant Plastic Travel Case, Protective Luggage with Foam Insert, Rebel Economy, 2041, 30.63"x11.52"x3.56" "Any product is only as strong as its weakest part." And the weakest part of this case are the latches. Although I didn't want to prove it to myself and ruin this Condition 1 case, the light plastic used and flimsy design will not hold up to any hard use.

I know that this is considered an "Economy Grade Case", but I wouldn't trust it to protect any expensive firearms. Please remember that "water resistant" doesn't mean "water proof", it should protect your weapon from rain but it can not be submerged. Also remember that any weapon stored either in a hard or a soft case will eventually rust and/or discolor unless it is allowed to breathe and air out on occasion. It is amazing how badly a stored firearm can look after being kept in a humid environment for any length of time.

Dropping this case on a hard surface will eventually cause the case to fail if anything of any weight is placed within it. That of course is not what this case is designed for and you shouldn't accidently drop it from anything above shoulder height. While this might provide adequate protection for inexpensive weapons I am always surprised when a manufacturer tries to enter into the lowest end of the market when their standard products already have a good reputation.
text_fidelity_b: Condition 1 30” Case, Hard Lockable Storage Box, Water Resistant Plastic Travel Case, Protective Luggage with Foam Insert, Rebel Economy, 2041, 30.63"x11.52"x3.56"

text_fidelity_a:
Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology I decided to pick one of these up from a local dealer about two months ago because I hate going to the gym. I reasoned that if I had a treadmill in my apartment, I would have NO more excuses when it came to working out. Luckily, this has paid off for me - I've used the treadmill nearly every day since it was delivered. I really love this treadmill so far.

The Precor was more expensive than similar models, but they seem to have a better reputation when it comes to quality, reliability, customer service, and repairs when things DO go wrong.

When I was testing out treadmills at the store, the Precor definitely did feel more sturdy and well built, even though it's one of their cheaper, Chinese made models. And even though the 9.23 is made in China, I was told that replacement parts are stocked in the US (if that means anything to anyone).

I use my treadmill for walking on an incline only. The manual says that it supports users up to 550 pounds for walking only, and 350 pounds for running (which is much higher than other, cheaper models). I started using the treadmill when I was about 330 pounds, and have never had any major problems with it (I'm down 8 pounds last time I checked). The motor doesn't jerk or hesitate at all, even for someone as heavy as me.

One thing to note regarding the maximum weight: the dealer told me to add 50 pounds to the maximum if you're going to run, so I would have exceeded the 350 pound max if I had done so. This didn't bother me though as I had only planned on walking at an incline anyway.

The only minor issue I've had so far is a slight bit of belt slippage under my right foot. There isn't anything in the manual about this, but after doing some research, I figured out how to tighten the belt a bit so this wouldn't happen. The belt would also go off center as well due to it being too loose. I haven't had a problem since tightening it.

The manual talks about centering the belt using the bolt on the right side of the belt only. To tighten the belt, you just have to do equal clockwise turns on each side of the belt while the treadmill is set to around 3 MPH - maybe a quarter or eighth turn at a time making sure the belt stays centered. I was very conservative about this, testing for slippage after each small turn, and I didn't have to tighten the belt much. This was pretty easy, but Precor will have the local repair people come out if you are at all uncomfortable doing this yourself.

I also called Precor customer service about the belt slippage just to be safe, and I also wanted to see how that whole process would go. When I called, I got connected to someone in the US nearly right away. The customer service agent directed me to the local repair guy, who confirmed what I had found about tightening the belt (he didn't need to come out). The agent seemed rather knowledgable about the product, and cleared up some wrong information I got from the dealer as well. So far, I'm pretty happy with Precor customer service.

The dealer told me I'd need to lubricate the belt, but the manual for the 9.23 says you never need to do this. Customer service confirmed that the 9.23's belt does NOT need to be lubricated.

The sound of the treadmill running and my footsteps are rather loud, but nothing too annoying when you wear headphones and listen to music. If others are in the room, it might be disturbing to them though.

The treadmill has a rather strong odor to it at first that DOES seem to diminish over time. The best way I can describe it is a plastic and/or electronics smell. It's not terrible, but it's not exactly lovely either.

The electronics are ultra basic - just what I wanted. You get a few programs and start, stop, incline and speed controls and that's it. I actually prefer this since I only ever use manual controls anyway, and I have other gadgets I use to do anything fancy.

The 9.23 doesn't have side rails, which is a bit uncomfortable at first, but I've gotten used to it. The next model up has rails and a few other things, but I didn't think it was worth the extra cost even though I really would prefer rails in order to steady myself. This is a minor issue that I've learned to live with.

There is a small ledge under the screen that's perfect for a Kindle or a tablet. I have a [[ASIN:B00HWMPSFQ Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 10.1 Tablet (Black)]], and it sits securely on the ledge even at 6% incline. I listen to music and use the Kindle app to read, or I listen to Audible audiobooks, and the time flies by. I have little trouble motivating myself to walk in the mornings.

The treadmill has a built-in heart rate monitor when you grip the handles. I have found this to be practically useless though, as the reading jumps up and down way too much, and it takes way too long to get a reading. I wanted to track heart rate, so I bought the Polar H7 heart rate sensor and paired it to my phone, and I use the Polar Beat app to track heart rate, time, and calories burned. So far I'm really loving this system.

The last thing I'll mention has more to do with modern circuit breakers than the treadmill itself. When I first got the treadmill, turning it on would trip adjacent breakers if there was a certain load above maybe around 100 watts on it, like a bathroom light and fan for example. I had never heard of a device tripping a DIFFERENT circuit breaker, but apparently this is very common with treadmills.

Apparently, treadmill motors emit some type of interference that trips newer types of circuit breakers (AFCI). Luckily there is an easy fix for this - all you have to do is plug the treadmill into a [[ASIN:B0000513O4 Tripp Lite ISOBAR4ULTRA Isobar Surge Protector Metal 4 Outlet 6 feet Cord 3330 Joules]] or something similar. I've also tried the [[ASIN:B0000510R4 Tripp Lite ISOBLOK2-0 2-Outlet Isobar Premium Surge Protector 1410 Joules]] but it didn't work. I know other similar surge protectors with EFI/RFI line noise filtering have been reported to work too, but I've only tried the Tripp Lite.

Overall, I'm really glad I spent the extra money on the Precor. It feels sturdy and meets my basic needs, and I have confidence that if I do have a problem, I'll be able to get it taken care of without a ton of hassle.
text_fidelity_b: Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology

Aquasana Premium Borosilicate Glass Bottle with Designer Silicone Sleeve and BPA Free Lid with Stainless Steel Cover, 550ml, Blue I've wanted a glass bottle for some time, so I was excited to get this. It's 9" tall, a 2.75" diameter at the bottom, and holds about 18 fluid ounces. The bottle is made from borosilicate glass, so it's strong (for glass) and more resistant to heat or cold shock than soda-lime glass. The outer, threaded part on the lid contains plastic, but the parts that contact the liquid are a metal inner "plug" and an O-ring. The lid is easy to screw on (and I have weak hands). I've not had any leaks when the bottle tips over with the lid on.

The mouth of the bottle is 1 1/8" across on the inside. If you're getting water from the faucet, it's easy enough to fill the bottle. I've ended up using a funnel when filling the bottle with my hot tea, though, as I apparently don't have a consistently steady hand. I can get a bottle brush into the bottle's mouth, though you can also put the bottle through the dish washer.

I've got size "medium womens" hands, and I've never felt like I might drop the bottle as the cross-hatch silicone sleeve design provides a good grip. The bottom of the sleeve covers the entire bottom of the bottle, which provides some padding and non-slip effect. The cross-hatch design allows my fingers to contact the hot (from my tea) side, though. I just wait for the tea to cool, but that might not be convenient for some people. Obviously, this bottle isn't insulated, so the liquid will cold or warm up to room temperature fairly quickly. It's a nice bottle.

Allen Sports Deluxe 2-Bike Trunk Mount Rack, Model ZN102, Black I bought an Allen bike rack 2 years ago and then just another for a friend this week. I didn't realize that my first bike rack has a Lifetime Guarantee, so I contacted Allen because the red rubber cradles dried and cracked after just one year of use. Allen said these are "wear and tear" items and I need to buy replacements. Well this 2 bike carrier cost me $32. The 4 replacement cradles I need are $6.50 a piece and shipping is $14.50 for a total of $40.50. I might as well just buy a brand new unit.

Why can't Allen sell just the red rubber parts that wear out (instead of the metal part that never wears out)? Because their money is in the replacement parts every year.

Their reply:
"Weather conditions are a major factor in the wear and tear of the item which is why the instructions sheet states: “Remove when not in use”. Unfortunately, we can not cover these parts under warranty. "
text_fidelity_b: Allen Sports Deluxe 2-Bike Trunk Mount Rack, Model ZN102, Black

EZX by EZ Lab EZX-SU361775GY Slim Under The Desk Electric Folding Quiet Anti-Shock Treadmill Hydraulic Armrest Home Office Exercise Body Induction Smart, Gray, 55" x 28.5" x 52" I was hesitant about purchasing this but, I decided to take a risk after seeing comparables online that were more expensive. The treadmill stores easily on the wall and I can move it into place whenever I want to use it. It is easy to control the roll even on a hardwood floor.

For Setup:
1. Place a little lube between the platform and running belt (Oil is included)

For Use:
1. Best to use on a hard surface (Hardwood / Tile)
2. Plug in Treadmill (Fold Handle Up if Needed - Highly suggested for initial use)
3. Stand on the end opposite of the digital readouts
4. Slowly take THREE steps forward (3 dashes stacked up on top of each other will appear on the digital readout)
5. The treadmill will slowly begin to move and continue to increase speed while you walk close to the readout screen
6. To hold a certain speed, walk on the middle section of the treadmill
7. To slow down, walk on the end furthest away from the digital readout
8. Keep in mind the machine will continue to speed up when you walk closest to the digital readout AND it will continue to slow down when you walk furthest from the readout, until it comes to a stop
9. If it comes to a stop and you want to continue your session, step off the treadmill and go back to step 3 of this section

It does take practice to get familiar with the treadmill and how speed adjustments are made. During familiarization, I suggest using the support handle that is on the machine. This is not your typical treadmill that has speed adjustment buttons. Hence, it will take time getting used to how it operates so be careful in the beginning.

For Belt Adjustment:
1. A wrench is included in the box
2. If the running belt tends to slide to the right during use, loosen the adjustment screw on the right side (the screw is on the opposite end of the digital readout)
3. If the running belt tends to slide to the left during use, loosen the adjustment screw on the left
4. Make 1/2 to 1/4 turn adjustments (extreme adjustments can make the tuning process more frustrating)
5. Take your time

I've always unplugged the machine after each use and store it against a wall. The running belt "ran" away from me a couple of times when I first got the treadmill and I prevented my fall by using the handrail. Every time I've had an issue with the speed on the treadmill, it's been due to operator error. I've had to remind myself and be cognizant of the fact that speed adjustments are done differently on this treadmill. I wanted something new, intuitive, easy to store, easy to move, and easy to operate. This treadmill met my criteria and is well designed and built.

I watched a lot of videos online before I purchased it. By the time it arrived, I was familiar with how to use it, what to avoid, and possible safety issues I'd have to keep in mind. I recommend this treadmill for OFFICE USE, WALKING, and LIGHT JOGS. For a workout, I recommend using a traditional treadmill with manual speed & incline adjustments.
text_fidelity_b: EZX by EZ Lab EZX-SU361775GY Slim Under The Desk Electric Folding Quiet Anti-Shock Treadmill Hydraulic Armrest Home Office Exercise Body Induction Smart, Gray, 55" x 28.5" x 52"

Minn Kota Endura C2 30 Freshwater Transom Mounted Trolling Motor (30" Shaft) What I meant by the catchy headline is that this is about the minimum horsepower for the small boat application. In my case I have it hooked to a Sun Dolphin 8.5 play boat. My calculation was that more power was not only not needed, but not wanted. I need those lower speeds for trolling and such. Also I need to make sure that when I go out I can get back in, less paddle.

Here is the deal. The thing is NOT a power hog. As of this writing (super rainy wet year) I have battled winds and currents in our overflowing rivers and having to stay on it all the time has been the test. I haven't got back to the pull out with less than a half battery yet.

My notion is that if you have a 14ft boat or less this engine is adequate. No need to break the bank if you're on a budget. For my purposes it is perfect!

The gadget that tilts the thing. Over the years I have fought with those releases. Not so on the MinnKota Endura Transom Mount Trolling Motor. Smoothest one I have ever seen.

The one thing that is not perfect is the reverse. Don't plan on running it from the front of the boat in reverse. Ain't happening. I don't know if the blades aren't pitched right or what, but the reverse really froths the water without giving much ooomph. I mean, it will back you out of the shallows, but it's not for full time use. Forward, on the other hand works just like you like.

About the handle.... Well, I wound up putting my trolling motor in the back and I was kinda worried about steering. You know, twisting around and all. But with the extension handle which you can pull out a lot or a little....it ended up being zero problem. I think I might actually like it more better on the aft now.

And one heads up. If you plan on putting a transducer onto the foot...be advised, it probably won't fit as the foot is too short. However...my workaround was to put my transducer all the way to the rear against the fin and shim it with some rubber pads on an edge so that I got it near to vertical. And my depth finder works just fine. So no harm done. You could use most anything that won't rot. Your wife's Tupperware, for instance.

I like my MinnKota Endura Transom Mount Trolling Motor a LOT and you will too. If your boat be smaller grab one. You'll be thankin' me!
text_fidelity_b: Minn Kota Endura C2 30 Freshwater Transom Mounted Trolling Motor (30" Shaft)

text_fidelity_a: 350W Electric Skateboard with Wireless Remote Control I am an old lady, not a skateboard person, but my neighbor is a divorced dad who gets his two boys every other weekend and because he has a roommate to help pay bills, I know he doesn't have a lot of money to spend on his kids when he gets them, so on occasion I have gotten a few things for them because I'd rather hear kids laughing and having fun than whining at their dad because he can't afford to buy them all the newest, coolest things.  So having said that, my intentions are also to benefit me, too!  I took this over before the boys were to be dropped off and he was so happy - I did apologize that I couldn't get two of them but hoped they would share.  About an hour later I heard them squealing so figured their dad had brought out this skateboard and was preparing to read them the riot act if they didn't share.  I looked up in time to see the older boy - he's maybe 10 or so - zoom past my house and the grin he had just made me laugh.  He was obviously loving the ride!  He came zooming past again and in another couple of minutes, the younger one - I think 7 or thereabouts - zoomed by.  His eyes were wide and he had the biggest grin on his face!  That's really all I wanted to see - that they liked it and I believe their dad was so happy to have a cool thing for them to play with at his house.  I mean, I can't say how it feels to be on it or anything like that, but I can say that two little boys had a fun weekend with their dad riding, I'm pretty sure, was their first ever skateboard and it was motorized and could be controlled with the remote control to boot!  If you are a grandparent or a parent of a young person (10 or younger, in my opinion), this skateboard is going to be a perfect gift for Christmas or their birthday.
text_fidelity_b: 350W Electric Skateboard with Wireless Remote Control
